opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest lesson was that a great open-source technology and a great business are two very different things. When we started Taichi Graphics, the excitement was real. The compiler worked, the community was growing, and people were writing beautiful physics simulations in a few hundred lines of Python. So it felt natural to assume that if enough people loved the tool, a business would follow.

What I learned is that a programming language sits very deep in the stack, and the further you are from the end user's actual problem, the harder it is to capture value. Developers love free, open infrastructure. That's part of why they adopt it. But when you ask who will pay, and for what, the answer gets complicated. Researchers and students, who were our most passionate users, usually don't have budgets. Large companies that do have budgets often want a complete solution for their specific workflow, not a compiler they then have to build on top of.

We tried different directions: tools around simulation, content creation, ways to make the technology more accessible to people who weren't hardcore programmers. Each one taught us something, but it also showed me that to make a product people would pay for, you have to obsess over a very specific customer and their pain, sometimes much more than over the elegance of the technology. As a researcher, my instinct was always "how do we make this more general, more powerful?" As a founder, the question had to become "who exactly is this for, and why would they pay for it tomorrow?"

So my conclusion was not that Taichi failed. I'm still very proud of it, and it's being used in research and education. The conclusion was more personal: I learned to separate building something technically beautiful from building something the market needs right now. Those can overlap, but you can't assume they do. And I learned a lot about myself — what I'm good at, what I need to grow in, and what kind of problems I really want to spend the next ten years on.

r001.rationale: The response says it was difficult to capture value from Taichi as open-source infrastructure and discusses seeking specific customer problems, but it does not state that contract work was the only viable commercialization path.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that I learned a general-purpose programming language is a very hard thing to sell, no matter how good it is technically.

When we started Taichi Graphics, the logic felt obvious. Taichi had a lot of users, people were building physics simulations and graphics pipelines with it, and I assumed that enthusiasm would translate into a business. But a language is infrastructure. People happily use it, they thank you, and then they build their own thing on top of it. The value gets captured by the application layer, not by the layer underneath. It's a bit like being the person who made the road. Everyone drives on it, nobody wants to pay a toll.

So we tried to move up the stack. We looked at offering simulation as a product, tooling, a cloud offering, things in that direction. And that taught me the second lesson, which is that the users who loved Taichi were not actually one market. There were game developers, researchers, visual effects people, robotics folks, each with very different needs and very different willingness to pay. A language can serve all of them because it's generic. A product cannot. The moment you specialize to make something sellable, you lose the breadth that made the open-source project exciting in the first place.

The third thing I'd say, and this one is more personal, is that I underestimated how different the skills are. Writing a compiler that generates good GPU code is a problem where if you're smart and you work hard, you make progress. Figuring out who your customer is, how to price, how to get a procurement department to say yes, that's not a problem that rewards cleverness in the same way. I was a researcher trying to be a founder, and the gap was real.

So what did I conclude? Mostly that open source and commercialization are two different projects that happen to share code. If I did it again, I would decide much earlier which one I was actually building, and I'd start from a concrete painful problem that a specific group of people would pay to solve, and then ask whether the technology helps, rather than starting from technology I was proud of and looking for a problem. That sounds obvious when you say it out loud. It's much less obvious when you've spent years building something you love.

r001.rationale: The response does not state that contract work was the only viable commercialization path. It discusses product offerings and concludes that open source and commercialization are separate projects.

astra-6.text: What I took away was that a useful technology isn’t automatically a viable business. With Taichi, we were starting from a technology we were excited about and trying to find a market for it. Commercialization pushed me to think in the opposite direction: what problem do people urgently need solved, and are they willing to pay for the solution? Technical sophistication alone doesn’t answer those questions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses finding a market and willingness to pay, but does not state that contract work was the only viable way to commercialize Taichi.

sol-6.1.text: My attempts to commercialize Taichi led me to realize that technical innovation alone isn’t enough to build a business. Taichi could make certain computations much faster, but that didn’t automatically translate into something customers urgently needed or were willing to pay for. You have to start with a concrete problem and understand the value of solving it. That changed how I thought about entrepreneurship: instead of starting with a technology and looking for applications, I needed to start with the customer’s needs.

r001.rationale: The response says commercialization required starting with customer needs, but does not state that contract work was the only viable way to commercialize Taichi.
